name: Aaron Zhang

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I'm from the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to employers, unions, AI firms or government. Your answers stay confidential. Describe a normal workday.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm Aaron Zhang, 58, and I've built and repaired power lines since my vocational certificate and apprenticeship. I know the worn switch at West Hill, like a job with a clear finish, and keep a printed circuit sheet in the truck; I have never used AI tools.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: The last label digit wore away and the tablet image did not help. A signed paper record and meter reading told us which circuit we actually had.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Now let's talk about AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the crew a shorter fault form is fine, but the line still has to be isolated and tested. I can live with paperwork moving faster.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I don't see much danger to my own job in that picture. My pay is about normal for line work, Lina's alterations shop has regular customers, and we have two months of bills saved.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'll keep taking the normal repair rota and put the same amount into our household savings each pay day. In the first year I'd keep the paper switching sheet in the truck and check the new forms against it; I've never used AI tools myself.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel settled enough. Our grown children have moved out, and Lina and I can handle a quiet month at the shop without missing rent.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: When did you need the paper sheet?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The West Hill switch label was worn, and our tablet image did not show its last digit. The signed paper copy and a meter check settled the circuit before we worked.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell a new worker about it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Read the number aloud to another crew member before moving a switch. A fast screen is no excuse for skipping a slow check.

say: I'd accept **shorter fault forms** after line repairs.
I'd keep **isolation checks** and paper switching records in the truck.
think: Our **typical line pay** and two months saved make a mild change manageable.
Lina's **regular alterations work** brings a second income for now.
do: Keep the **normal repair rota** and existing savings transfer.
Check **new forms** against the signed paper switching sheet in the first year.
feel: **Settled** about income and the ordinary workday.
S0.quote: A fast screen is no excuse for skipping a slow check.
fieldNote: Aaron's **paper backup** helped resolve a worn switch label, explaining his preference without implying fear of all paperwork change.
Two months of **savings** and Lina's current orders make the mild scenario feel manageable to him.

steps.text: Continue normal line repairs and existing household savings transfers

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Now let's talk about Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the depot to let dispatchers test any planning software against real faults before shifting their work. A machine route should never override the signed switching order.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I expect field crews to remain because robots move slowly here, and Lina still has customers who want fittings by hand. I'd worry more about losing local dispatch knowledge than about our pay in the next year.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Now I'd ask our dispatcher to print one new route beside the existing feeder map after the office has tried the system. In the first year I'd keep normal line shifts and report any mismatch at West Hill to the supervisor instead of using the AI tool myself.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel uneasy for the people who know the roads, not in immediate danger at home. I won't call a new screen safe because it made a good first impression.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What might a route miss at West Hill?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The service lane closes for the morning market, so the truck uses the rear approach. Our dispatcher knows the hours and tells us before we leave.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you oppose the system after a successful trial?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No, if the dispatcher and crew check the results, I can follow the printed route. I don't have to become a software user to accept a useful direction.

say: I'd request **dispatcher trials** against real faults before staff changes.
I'd keep **signed switching orders** above machine routes.
think: Our **hands-on wages** look safe while robots spread slowly.
I worry about **local dispatch knowledge** disappearing from field instructions.
do: Compare a **printed route** with the feeder map after office testing.
Keep **normal line shifts** and report West Hill mismatches to the supervisor.
feel: **Uneasy** for dispatch staff, without immediate household income danger.
S1.quote: I don't have to become a software user to accept a useful direction.
fieldNote: Aaron distinguishes **using a printed result** from personally adopting AI, consistent with never having used AI tools.
The **morning-market closure** gives him a concrete dispatch concern, while his household wages still look safe.

steps.text: Continue paid line shifts and compare printed routes with feeder maps

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Now let's talk about AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the company thinking AI in 2028 may write plans, but robots around 2031 could repair lines and sew clothes. We need the staffing dates and safety rules in writing before either of us changes work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'll be 63 when robots arrive and may still need the line wage. Lina's alterations work could face the same hands-on machines, and our two-month reserve is not enough for both of us to stop.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Now I'd request a written retirement estimate and ask the company which line jobs it expects to keep after the robot trials. In 2029 I'd apply for a paid inspection course if it offers a recognised certificate; in the first robot year I'd apply for posted field-checking roles here and at the other utilities within commuting distance.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel anxious about both wages, though I can ask and apply before the date. I won't leave my current shift on an untested promise that a new post exists.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you ask Lina at home?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask my partner Lina to list slow months at the alterations shop, not just the wedding-season rush. Our grown children have families of their own and cannot be our retirement plan.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why inspection work?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I've checked completed repairs for younger crew members, so I know what a sound connection looks like. A robot may eventually check itself, which is why I would only trust a posted job with actual pay.

say: I'd separate **2028 planning AI** from 2031 hands-on robots.
I'd request **written staffing dates** and robot safety rules.
think: At **63**, I may still need my line wage.
Lina's **alterations income** could face robots, making two months saved too short.
do: Request a **retirement estimate** and written post-trial staffing plans now.
Apply for a **paid inspection course** if offered in 2029, then seek posted field-checking jobs in 2031.
feel: **Anxious** about two wages, with applications still possible.
S2.quote: I won't leave my current shift on an untested promise that a new post exists.
fieldNote: Aaron expects **robot risk at 2031** for both line repair and alterations, while thinking AI changes plans earlier.
His **course condition** is paid training with a recognised certificate, and his job search depends on posted wages.

steps.text: Request written retirement and post-trial staffing figures
Apply for a paid inspection course in 2029 if recognised
Apply for posted field-checking jobs at commuting utilities in 2031

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Now let's talk about AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell management five years is enough to run a trial on real lines and let workers see the results. Thinking AI arrives in 2031, and field robots around 2034, when I'll be 66.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At 66 I could perhaps retire, but I don't know the income until I see the statement and count Lina's quieter shop months. If sewing machines replace some fittings, we may still need paid work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This year I'd request retirement figures for both of us and ask the foreman to include the worn West Hill switch in any robot trial. In 2032 I'd take a paid safety-inspection placement if it is offered; in 2034 I'd retire only if a low-income budget covers us, otherwise apply for posted inspection shifts.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel more room to consider the choices, though I dislike guessing about the shop. Five years means we can check the figures before making a promise to ourselves.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would the trial need to show?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A robot should stop when the worn label cannot be read and ask a crew to confirm the circuit. I want the meter reading on the same record as the image.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What is in the low-income budget?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Housing, medicines and Lina's slow months between wedding seasons. I wouldn't count the busiest fitting week as normal income.

say: I'd request **real-line trials** and shared results before 2034.
I'd distinguish **2031 thinking AI** from field robots three years later.
think: Retirement at **66** depends on written income figures from the retirement office.
Lina's **quiet shop months** matter if alterations work shrinks.
do: Get **retirement figures** and request a West Hill switch trial.
Take a **paid inspection placement** if offered in 2032; retire or seek posted shifts in 2034.
feel: **Less rushed**, still uncertain about the shop's income.
S3.quote: I want the meter reading on the same record as the image.
fieldNote: Aaron's **2034 choice** depends on a low-income budget for Lina's shop and an actual pension figure.
His **trial criterion** is an unreadable switch label paired with a human stop rule and measured voltage.

steps.text: Compare written retirement figures with quiet-month alterations income
Take a paid safety-inspection placement in 2032 if offered
Apply for posted inspection shifts if retirement income falls short

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Now let's talk about AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell younger crews ten years is enough to keep clear records of old switches before the machines use them. Thinking AI arrives in 2036 and field robots around 2039, when I'll be 71.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I expect I could retire before 71 if the statements cover our home and medicines. Lina's alterations work may change with robots around 2039, but we have time to check the shop figures before choosing a date.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Now I'd keep working paid repairs and ask for updated retirement statements each year. In 2037 Lina and I would settle a date if a low-income budget fits; by 2039 I'd hand the newer crew my West Hill switch notes and apply for posted inspection hours if our numbers still fall short.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel calm about my own income for the next few years and watchful about the long plan. Ten years gives us a chance to decide with figures rather than a headline.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would the switch notes include?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The last digit of the West Hill label is worn, so I'd mark the correct circuit number and the meter reading on paper. A new worker should not guess from a blurry image.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you ask the children to help finance retirement?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No, our grown children visit often, but they have their own households. We would delay my retirement before asking them to carry our bills.

say: I'd urge crews to keep **old switch records** through the decade.
I'd note **2039 robots** reach field repairs when I'll be 71.
think: Retirement before **71** looks possible if verified income covers household costs.
Lina's **alterations work** may change later and belongs in the forecast.
do: Keep **paid repairs** and update retirement statements annually.
Set a **2037 date** if bills fit; hand over West Hill notes and seek inspection hours if needed.
feel: **Calm** about near-term wages, watchful about the longer household plan.
S4.quote: A new worker should not guess from a blurry image.
fieldNote: Aaron expects **retirement before 2039** to be possible with verified figures, rather than assuming the robot date protects his job.
His **switch notes** preserve a worn digit and measured circuit number for newer crews and possible robots.

steps.text: Continue paid line repairs and update retirement statements annually
Choose a 2037 retirement date only if low-income figures cover bills
Apply for posted inspection hours if retirement income falls short

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028 worries me most because robots around 2031 could reach both my line repairs and Lina's alterations work. Written staffing dates, paid recognised training, posted local jobs and honest retirement figures would help us decide.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Ask who tells a robot to stop when a label cannot be read. A clear stop rule matters more than a tidy demonstration.

headlineQuote: A clear stop rule matters more than a tidy demonstration.
portrait: Aaron is a **58-year-old experienced lineworker** with a certificate and apprenticeship, typical pay and about two months saved.
He keeps **printed circuit records** after a worn West Hill label required a meter check and signed paper confirmation.
He **never uses AI tools** and will accept printed directions only after dispatchers and crews test a system.
The **2031 robot date** worries him because both line repairs and Lina's alterations income could change before retirement is affordable.
Longer warning gives him **retirement figures**, while he keeps paid repair work.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028** worries Aaron most because 2031 robots could affect his repair wage and Lina's alterations income.
whatWouldHelp: He wants **written staffing dates**, paid recognised training, real posted jobs and verified retirement figures.
